To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
allergen exposure increases T cell proliferation in all T cell subsets in the lungs, with the most expansion of GATA3+ Th2 cells.
allergen exposure increased the number of CD4+ T-bet+ (Th1), GATA-3 (Th2), RORγt (Th17), Foxp3+ (Tregs), and BrdU+ T cell subsets in the lung of allergen-challenged mice.

allergen exposure leads to the proliferation and expansion of all four T cell subsets (Th1, Th2 and Th17 and Tregs), with a dominant Th2 response, but with different cell distribution in the lung microenvironment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the expansion and proliferation of Th1, Th17, Th2 and Treg cells, and their local distribution in the lung, in response to allergen challenge.

the identification of the T cell subsets that contribute to allergic inflammation in the lung, the local distribution of these cells, and the local inflammatory milieu that regulates the presence and activity of these cells.
the localisation of different T cell subsets in the lung, and their relationship to local cytokine and chemokine expression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
allergen exposure increases T cell proliferation and localisation in the lung, which is accompanied by the local expression of a number of cytokine genes, chemokines, and chemokine receptor genes.
allergen challenge induces a mixed T-cell profile in the airways, which is characterised by a Th2 dominance, but also includes Th1, Th17 and regulatory T cells.
allergen exposure induces proliferation of all T cell subsets, with Th2 cells being the dominant T cells in allergic inflammation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
allergen exposure increases the expansion of Th2, Th1, Th17 and Foxp3 cells, with a dominant Th2 response, which is associated with a distinct local inflammatory microenvironment.
allergen exposure induces a local Th2 response with a dominant role of GATA- 3+ T cells, and that this response may be regulated by T-bet+ T cells, RORγ+ T cells and Foxp3 T cells.
the local inflammatory milieu is a key factor in regulating the expansion and distribution of T effector cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
allergen exposure increases T cell proliferation in the lung and that this is not restricted to one particular T cell subset.
all the T effector cells are involved in allergic airway inflammation.
allergen exposure increases the numbers of all T cell subsets, and that each T cell subset is differentially regulated and distributed in different microenvironments of the lung.
